title: Unity or Unreal? - same game, different quality and style
author: Old-Wolverine-4134
selftext:
I decided to replicate my Unity game in Unreal to see how it would look and work. Still not done tests how heavy is the game on each engine, but my bet is UE one is much more demanding. With that said, UE allows much more details and superb lighting and visuals. On other hand the unity style has it's own charm I guess.

Curious to hear your opinion which one is better.

comments.author: i_rate_slop
comments.body:
The fact that it’s even possible for you to test both game engines like this in a reasonable amount of time is fucking wild. Incredible times :)

Stick with Unity until you release unless UE really gives you something meaningful. Focus on fun gameplay. UE isn’t easy for coding agents and will use more tokens in total to achieve the same functionality. Can you do it in UE? Of course. Should you? Maybe not.

Do UE for Island Game 2. Maximize your chances of completing Island Game 1.

replies.author: nextnode
replies.body: How is Unity easier for LLMs than Unreal?

replies.author: i_rate_slop
replies.body:
LLMs are much better at C++ than they used to be, but it’s still much more verbose than C# and you end up with a lot more churn on issues before they arrive at a working solution.

Unity’s CLI is also much more token efficient than UEs MCP. If you don’t wrap the UE MCP yourself, coding agents will use a TON of tokens just negotiating what they’re allowed to do, not even doing useful work.

Lastly, Unity code is just simpler in general. Less opportunity for both you the developer and coding agents to get lost in the code. And the C# community’s fixation on clean code and hyper-rigid architectural patterns lends well to coding agents, compared to C++ where you are left to choose your own adventure most of the time.

So it’s not just that Unity is easier for LLMs. It’s simply easier overall and that maximizes your chance of success.

\-

I personally prefer UE, but I always start in Unity or Godot first, though. Never UE until I want MetaHumans.

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48

Unity wasn't initially designed for high performance.  Its initial appeal, pre-generative AI, was artist accessibility (allowing artists to do more without code) and its great cross platform support.

That said they added an ECS (Entity Component System) to address these issues about 2018 but not too many people use it becuase Unreal WAS designed with performance in mind. I would, however, be very curious about the following:

1. Did you start the Unity version long enough ago that you were using a different frontier model (or version)?
2. What would happen if you had the model try to make the Unity version more realistic (possibly specifying to use ECS)?

replies.author: Relevant-Positive-48
replies.body:
Can I ask when you started using Unity?

Back when it was first released many (and probably most) games were written either with internally built engines or using libraries that included very few, if any, integrated tools for artists.  They tended to be super performant because they were written directly in C or C++ but the asset pipeline was a mess and anything but standardized.

For Unity, the object-oriented approach and C# (and back then Javascript and Boo) scripted code meant a known performance hit next to raw C and C++ games but team productivity skyrocketed and porting costs were drastically reduced.

replies.author: SnuffleBag
replies.body:
I first used Unity professionally in 2008, but I think your timeline is a little bit shifted tbh.

Even if you go back to the initial release of Unity in 2005, gameplay code had already started transitioning away from native code and towards scripting languages and graph based logic. UnrealScript shipped with Unreal Engine in 1998, Kismet shipped with Unreal Engine 3 in 2004. Ubisoft had their own scripting and graph thing in the early 2000s. So did Activation and EA.

But even before this shift, gameplay code was very much object oriented in most engines, just written in C++ instead of C#/Unityscript. The Quake C style of global variables across the engine and flat transformation of data all but died when game programmers changed from being old demosceners and basement dwellers to mandatory college degrees.

In most games, gameplay code execution time is dwarfed by engine execution time, and Unity's engine code looks roughly like all the other engines on the market - it is written in C++ with sprinkles of assembly and intrinsics to be performant like all the other engines.

In that landscape, Unity's scripting solution was actually among the more performant of the options. Their object and data model is really what's been holding them back for all these years. It's hard to properly optimize something where all data is mutable at all times.

But then again you don't use Unity to make AAA games. Not then, not now.
